title: At the café
goal: Order drinks and food, and set up the first of the six cases: the accusative — the form a noun takes when it is the target of an action.
bekal: order in three ways: *prosím si*, *dám si*, and *chcel by som*
put any noun into the accusative — including knowing when it doesn't change at all
use the object pronouns *ma, ťa, ho, ju*

notes: **Prosím si and dám si — two ways to order, both with *si*.** The little word means "for oneself", so *dám si pivo* is literally "I'll give myself a beer". Slovaks almost always add it when ordering; leaving it out makes your sentence sound like a command.

**Kávu, not káva.** This is the accusative, the heart of this unit. Feminine nouns ending in *-a* change to *-u* when they are the target: *káva → kávu*, *voda → vodu*, *polievka → polievku*. It's the ending you'll need most in everyday life, and the quickest to feel natural.

**Pivo and koláč don't change.** Neuter nouns never change in the accusative, and neither do masculine nouns for **things**. So of the six groups of nouns, three ask nothing of you in this case. Good news that grammar books rarely mention.

**Pohár vody uses yet another form** — the genitive, for the contents of a container: "a glass of water". Just like *šálka kávy* (a cup of coffee) and *fľaša vína* (a bottle of wine). The form is set out in unit 9; for now learn it as a chunk.

**Jednu, jedno, jeden.** The number one behaves exactly like an adjective: it follows gender **and** case. *Jeden koláč* (m), *jedno pivo* (n), *jednu kávu* (f, accusative). Numbers from two up are far more relaxed, and they're covered in unit 5.

grammars.title: The accusative — the first of six cases
body: The accusative is the form a noun takes when it is the **direct target** of an action: what you order, see, buy, or have. Its questions are *koho?* (whom) and *čo?* (what).
The full rule fits in one table, and half its rows demand no change at all.
after: **The adjective changes along with its noun.** The endings: m animate **-ého** (*vidím dobrého učiteľa*), m inanimate **-ý** unchanged (*vidím veľký stôl*), f **-ú** (*prosím si veľkú kávu*), n **-é** unchanged (*dám si dobré pivo*).

**Why are male living beings different?** Because Slovak needs to tell who does what to whom, while its word order is very free. *Brat vidí otca* and *Otca vidí brat* both mean "the brother sees the father" — the ending decides, not the order. With things that confusion rarely arises, so the language doesn't bother.

**Verbs that take the accusative** are the ones with a target: *mať* (to have), *vidieť* (to see), *kupovať* (to buy), *prosiť si* (to ask for), *dať si* (to order), *hľadať* (to look for), *poznať* (to know someone), *piť* (to drink), *jesť* (to eat), *čítať* (to read), *písať* (to write).

grammars.title: Pronouns as objects
body: When the target is a person, the pronoun also has its own accusative form. Most are very short, and like *som* and *sa*, they are never stressed.
after: **The short form is used almost always**, and it takes **second place** in the sentence, right after the first word: *Ja ťa vidím*, *Zajtra ťa vidím*, *Vidím ťa*. It never stands at the start of a sentence.
**The long form is used only for emphasis** or after a preposition: *Mňa nevidíš?* ("You don't see **me**?"), *pre teba* (for you), *bez neho* (without him).

When two short words come in a row, the order is fixed: *som/si* first, then *sa/si*, then the object. *Videl som ťa* = "I saw you (yesterday)". The order becomes automatic once your ear is used to it, and until then, copy whole sentences.

blocks.title: Coffee in Slovakia
items: *Presso* or *espresso* = espresso. *Kapucíno* = cappuccino. *Viedenská káva* = coffee with whipped cream, a Viennese legacy that's still alive.
If you just order *káva*, you'll usually get a small espresso. For a longer coffee, ask for *veľká káva* or *lungo*.
*Turecká káva* still survives in old-style bars: ground coffee brewed right in the cup, unfiltered — strong, thick, and worth trying once.

blocks.text: Look at *zmrzlina*: a cluster of consonants up front, with no vowel letter until the second syllable. It's said *ZMRZ-lee-nah* — let the *r* carry the syllable. Slovak children learn to say it before most other words, because the reward is worth it.

sections.title: Three ways to order, from casual to most polite

blocks.text: **Prosím si** is the safest choice for beginners: polite without sounding stiff, and used by Slovaks themselves all day long. **Chcel/chcela by som** is the conditional — notice that it follows the gender of **the speaker**, not the listener. This is the only place in A1 where you have to know your own gender to choose a word.

head: More café phrases
English
rows: The bill, please. / I'd like to pay.

blocks.title: Two table customs worth knowing
items: **Dobrú chuť** is said before eating, by anyone to anyone at the table — including the waiter to the guests. The reply is *ďakujem, navzájom* ("thank you, same to you").

**Tips** are given by naming the rounded total as you pay, not by leaving money on the table. If the bill is €8.60 and you hand over ten euros saying *deväť* (nine), the waiter gives you one euro back and the rest is the tip. Usually five to ten percent.
